B12C130.summary: Yudhishthira asks what a weak, besieged king should do when his land is lost, his treasury is empty and his councils have leaked. Bhishma advises peace with an honest invader, and giving up land or even the capital to a treacherous one to save his life. If peace fails, the king should fight bravely, because a warrior who dies in battle goes to heaven.

scenes.B12C130S01: Yudhishthira asks about a king in ruin, and Bhishma answers with advice on peace, retreat and courageous fighting.

shots.B12C130S01H02: Yudhishthira asks what a weak king should do when his lands are taken, his wealth is gone and his allies cannot be supported.
shots.B12C130S01H03: Bhishma says an honest invader should be met with peace and the lost land restored, while a treacherous one may be bought off with land or even the capital.
shots.B12C130S01H04: Yudhishthira asks what a king should do when his own people turn against him, his treasury is empty and his counsels are leaked.
shots.B12C130S01H05: Bhishma advises peace with a righteous enemy and bold fighting against a wicked one, and says even a small loyal army can win or die honourably.

B12C131.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a Brahmana can make a living when proper rule has collapsed, robbers control the means of life, and he cannot abandon his family. Bhishma says he should live by his learning, and that in hard times a king may take wealth from the wicked and give it to the good. Even then the king must not oppress priests or Brahmanas, and he should not believe slander.

scenes.B12C131S01: Yudhishthira's question about a Brahmana's livelihood in a time of disorder, and Bhishma's long answer on conduct in distress.

shots.B12C131S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a Brahmana should support his family when righteous rule has broken down and robbers hold the means of living.
shots.B12C131S01H02: Bhishma says the Brahmana should live by knowledge, and that a king may seize wealth from the wicked for the good without provoking revolt, though he must never oppress Brahmanas, must not believe slander, and should bear his burdens steadily.

B12C132.summary: Bhishma explains that a king must keep his treasury full, drawing on his own realm and his enemies' lands by a middle course. He argues that a weak king with an empty purse loses respect and power, so he must not bend before enemies. On robbers, he advises bringing them under control rather than destroying them outright, since those who exterminate them live in fear.

scenes.B12C132S01: Bhishma's advice on filling the treasury, keeping a firm hand on the kingdom, and handling robbers.

shots.B12C132S01H01: Bhishma says a king must keep his treasury full, since a king without wealth loses respect, and he must deal firmly with robbers by bringing them under his rule rather than destroying them.

B12C133.summary: Bhishma says a Kshatriya's clear duties are religious merit and wealth, and that endless debate about the unseen future should not stop him from them. He argues that power is the foundation of righteousness and that the powerful can do much that the weak cannot. He then lists the penances by which a man who has fallen into sin can cleanse himself and win back respect.

scenes.B12C133S01: Bhishma on a Kshatriya's duties, the primacy of power over abstract righteousness, and the penance for one who has sinned.

shots.B12C133S01H01: Bhishma says a Kshatriya should pursue merit and wealth and seek power, since power sustains righteousness, and he lists the penances that cleanse a sinner.

B12C134.summary: Bhishma tells the story of Kayavya, a robber of mixed birth who was devout, protected Brahmanas and ascetics, and cared for his blind parents. When thousands of robbers choose him as their leader, he sets rules: spare women, children, ascetics and Brahmanas, and plunder only where it is due. Bhishma says that robbers who keep these rules win a good afterlife, and that hearing the tale brings safety from fear.

scenes.B12C134S01: The story of the robber Kayavya, his election as leader, the rules he sets, and the lesson Bhishma draws from it.

shots.B12C134S01H01: Bhishma introduces Kayavya, a skilled and devout robber who honours Brahmanas and his blind parents, and whom many robbers then wish to make their leader.
shots.B12C134S01H02: The robbers ask Kayavya to lead them and protect them the way a father or mother would.
shots.B12C134S01H03: Kayavya lays down rules: never kill women or non-combatants, spare Brahmanas, keep truth, and tax only those who refuse their dues.
shots.B12C134S01H04: Bhishma says the robbers obeyed Kayavya, prospered by giving up sin, and that hearing his story brings freedom from fear.

B12C135.summary: Bhishma quotes verses attributed to Brahman on how a king should fill his treasury. The wealth of sacrificers and of the gods must not be taken, but wealth of those who neglect sacrifice may be taken for the army and for worship, and the king should pass it on to good people rather than hoard it. He ends by comparing moral questions to dust that grows finer the more it is ground.

scenes.B12C135S01: Bhishma quotes Brahman's verses on which wealth a king may take, and closes with a comparison about moral questions.

shots.B12C135S01H01: Bhishma quotes verses of Brahman that allow a king to take wealth from those who neglect sacrifice but protect the wealth of sacrificers and temples, and says that moral questions grow finer the more they are discussed.

B12C136.summary: Bhishma tells a fable of three Sakula fish in a lake that fishermen are draining. One fish sees the danger and leaves early, another escapes by biting the string when caught, and the slow one is caught and dies. Bhishma's lesson is that foresight and quick thinking bring success, procrastination brings ruin, and well-timed action gets the best results.

scenes.B12C136S01: Bhishma's fable of the three fish and the lesson on acting in time.

shots.B12C136S01H01: Bhishma tells how three fish face draining water: the far-sighted one leaves early, the quick-witted one escapes by feigning capture, and the slow one is caught and dies.
shots.B12C136S01H02: Bhishma draws the lesson that procrastinators are destroyed, that foresight and presence of mind bring happiness, and that acting with regard to time and place wins the best results.

B12C137.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a weak king surrounded by many foes should choose friends and enemies, and when to make war or peace. Bhishma answers with the fable of a mouse and a cat caught in the same hunter's net, in which the mouse makes a timely alliance with the cat, frees him, and then refuses his later offer of friendship. The moral is that alliances rest on self-interest, so a ruler should seem trusting while staying wary, and should act at the right time.

scenes.B12C137S01: Yudhishthira's question about a besieged king, and the fable of the mouse Palita and the cat Lomasa, which ends with the mouse rejecting the cat's offer of friendship.
scenes.B12C137S02: The cat, shamed, pleads for renewed friendship, and the mouse answers with advice to keep a steady distrust of everyone.

shots.B12C137S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a weak king under attack from many powerful foes can choose friends and enemies and decide when to fight or make peace.
shots.B12C137S01H02: Bhishma replies that friends can turn into foes and back, so a king should sometimes make peace with enemies, and he introduces the tale of a cat and a mouse under a banyan tree.
shots.B12C137S01H03: The mouse Palita lives beneath a banyan where the cat Lomasa hunts birds, and the cat is caught in a hunter's net; seeing a mongoose and an owl waiting for himself, the mouse decides to strike a deal with the cat.
shots.B12C137S01H04: The grateful cat agrees to serve the mouse and accept the alliance, and the mouse says he will cut the net if the cat spares his life.
shots.B12C137S01H05: The mouse cuts the net slowly, then flees when the hunter arrives, and when the cat later asks for friendship the mouse refuses, arguing that all bonds rest on self-interest.
shots.B12C137S02H01: The cat, rebuked, is ashamed and speaks up.
shots.B12C137S02H02: The cat protests his loyalty and asks the mouse to renew their friendship, but the mouse refuses, advises constant mistrust, and slips into another hole.
shots.B12C137S02H03: Bhishma draws the morals: appear fearless while distrusting others, make peace with foes when it suits, and honour Brahmanas, and he urges Yudhishthira to act with the same wisdom.

B12C138.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a king can rule if he trusts no one, and Bhishma answers with the tale of the bird Pujani and King Brahmadatta. After the prince kills her chick, Pujani blinds him in revenge, and the two then argue over whether an injury can ever be forgiven. Brahmadatta appeals to Time and to reconciliation, while Pujani holds that enmity between injurer and injured never truly ends, so she leaves; the tale closes with advice that a king should protect his subjects and never provoke a stronger foe.

scenes.B12C138S01: Yudhishthira's doubt about mistrust, and the story of the prince who kills Pujani's chick and her revenge on him, which ends with an argument over whether the score is settled.
scenes.B12C138S02: The two argue over whether a wronged party can ever trust the one who wronged them, and whether living together softens hostility.
scenes.B12C138S03: Brahmadatta blames Time for all acts, Pujani answers with a long case for exertion and good rule, and she takes her leave.

shots.B12C138S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a king can rule and fight his foes if he may trust no one.
shots.B12C138S01H02: Bhishma introduces the bird Pujani, who lived at King Brahmadatta's palace and fed her chick and the prince on fruit, until the prince killed her chick and she blinded him in revenge.
shots.B12C138S01H03: Brahmadatta says the injury has been repaid and the account is squared, and he asks Pujani to stay.
shots.B12C138S01H04: Pujani says that a wrongdoer should leave the wronged party, that soothing words should not be trusted, and that enmity passes down to descendants.
shots.B12C138S01H05: Brahmadatta insists that avenging an injury is no offence and again asks her to stay.
shots.B12C138S02H01: Pujani says that friendship cannot be rebuilt once one side has injured the other and the other has struck back.
shots.B12C138S02H02: Brahmadatta argues that injurer and avenger should unite, since mutual hatred has been seen to cool that way.
shots.B12C138S02H03: Pujani replies that enmity never dies, and that insincere conciliation can subdue even the strong.
shots.B12C138S02H04: Brahmadatta says that living together softens hostility, citing the Chandala and the dog, and that animosity fades quickly.
shots.B12C138S02H05: Pujani lists five causes of hostility, says the fire of enmity burns until one party is destroyed, and says she cannot trust him again.
shots.B12C138S03H01: Brahmadatta says Time causes all acts and deaths, so no one is truly to blame, and he asks her to forgive and stay.
shots.B12C138S03H02: Pujani challenges his view by asking why people avenge, why physicians treat the sick and why rites matter if Time rules all, then describes the miseries of life and warns against trusting a wronged foe.
shots.B12C138S03H03: Brahmadatta replies that withholding trust wins no object and that fear makes a man as good as dead.
shots.B12C138S03H04: Pujani argues that exertion matters more than fate, lists the marks of wisdom, and says she will leave a bad king's realm; she then describes a just king who protects his subjects and a tyrant who brings ruin on himself.
shots.B12C138S03H05: Bhishma closes that Pujani has taken her leave and gone away, and asks Yudhishthira what else he would like to hear.

B12C139.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a king should act when righteousness and people have declined and robbers plague the land. Bhishma tells how Satrunjaya, king of the Sauviras, asked the sage Bharadwaja how to gain, grow, guard and use wealth. Bharadwaja replies that a ruler must rely on firm punishment, cut the roots of his foes, and mix sternness, mildness and deceit as the moment requires, and the king prospers by following this advice.

scenes.B12C139S01: Yudhishthira asks about kingship in an age of decline, and Bhishma gives Bharadwaja's advice to King Satrunjaya on statecraft in hard times.

shots.B12C139S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a king should behave when righteousness and people decay and robbers overrun the land.
shots.B12C139S01H02: Bhishma says he will teach the policy for hard times, and introduces King Satrunjaya of the Sauviras, who asks the sage Bharadwaja how wealth is gained, increased, guarded and used.
shots.B12C139S01H03: Bharadwaja advises the king to keep the rod of punishment raised, to cut out his enemies' roots, to act humbly only in speech, to make and break alliances as needed, and to match sternness or mildness to the occasion.
shots.B12C139S01H04: Bhishma says the king followed this advice gladly and won prosperity for himself and his kin.

B12C140.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a Brahmana and a king should live when righteousness has collapsed and famine and robbery have overrun the land. Bhishma tells of the sage Viswamitra, who in a twelve-year drought steals a dog's haunch from a Chandala's hut to stay alive. The Chandala argues at length that the meat is unclean and the theft sinful, but Viswamitra answers with hunger, precedent and the claim that saving life comes first, then eats the meat after offering it to the gods. The story teaches that a wise man may act against normal rules to survive great distress, and can later regain his merit.

scenes.B12C140S01: Yudhishthira's question, the account of the famine that drives Viswamitra to the Chandala's hut, and the sage's first theft attempt and plea.
scenes.B12C140S02: The Chandala says only certain animals are clean food, and Viswamitra cites Agastya's precedent to justify eating the dog's meat.
scenes.B12C140S03: Viswamitra argues that a sage cannot sin and that his body must be kept alive, and the Chandala answers that hunger must be conquered.
scenes.B12C140S04: The Chandala tries to restrain the sage as a friend, and Viswamitra asks to be saved by giving up the meat, which the Chandala refuses.
scenes.B12C140S05: Viswamitra argues that saving life outweighs the sin of unclean food, and the Chandala says he is ignoring the Veda and the code of the Aryas.
scenes.B12C140S06: The Chandala gives a final warning, and Viswamitra takes the meat, offers it to the gods and ancestors, and eats it.

shots.B12C140S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a Brahmana and a king should live when righteousness has collapsed and famine, robbery and lawlessness prevail.
shots.B12C140S01H02: Bhishma says the king's conduct shapes the age, and tells how Viswamitra, starving after a twelve-year drought, wandered until he reached a Chandala hamlet and found a dog's haunch in a hut.
shots.B12C140S01H03: The Chandala challenges the intruder, Viswamitra admits he came to steal the meat out of hunger, and the Chandala warns that the theft and the unclean food are sinful.
shots.B12C140S01H04: The Chandala says the meat would cost the sage his long life and strength, and tells him to seek other food.
shots.B12C140S01H05: Viswamitra replies that no other meat can be had in famine, he has no money, and the dog's haunch seems to him to contain all six tastes.
shots.B12C140S02H01: The Chandala says that only certain five-clawed animals are clean food for the twice-born, and warns the sage away from unclean food.
shots.B12C140S02H02: Viswamitra cites Agastya, who ate the demon Vatapi while hungry, as a precedent for eating the haunch.
shots.B12C140S02H03: The Chandala says the act is wrong, asks him to seek other alms, and grudgingly allows him to take the meat if he insists.
shots.B12C140S02H04: Viswamitra says the good set the standard for duty, and that he now judges the dog's haunch better than any pure food.
shots.B12C140S02H05: The Chandala replies that an unrighteous act cannot become a lasting custom, and urges him not to sin by deceit.
shots.B12C140S03H01: Viswamitra says a Rishi cannot do wrong and that deer and dog are alike as animals, so he will eat the haunch.
shots.B12C140S03H02: The Chandala argues that Agastya acted at the request of Brahmanas, that righteousness is what is free of sin, and that Brahmanas should be kept alive.
shots.B12C140S03H03: Viswamitra says his body is dear to him and must be sustained, and that his hunger makes him fearless of the Chandala and his kin.
shots.B12C140S03H04: The Chandala says men give up their lives rather than eat unclean food, and that conquering hunger brings the highest rewards.
shots.B12C140S03H05: Viswamitra says he has kept strict vows and will eat the meat to protect the root of merit, and that the act is clean for a pure soul even if it is wrong.
shots.B12C140S04H01: The Chandala says he must restrain the sage, since a Brahmana who does wrong falls from his high state.
shots.B12C140S04H02: Viswamitra replies that cows drink no matter what frogs croak, and tells the Chandala not to claim authority over what is right.
shots.B12C140S04H03: The Chandala says he speaks only as a friend and asks the sage to do what is good and avoid temptation.
shots.B12C140S04H04: Viswamitra asks the Chandala, as a friend, to rescue him by giving up the haunch, so that he might be saved by righteousness rather than sin.
shots.B12C140S04H05: The Chandala refuses either to give or to let him take the meat, since both of them would sink to hell if a Brahmana ate it.
shots.B12C140S05H01: Viswamitra says he will sin now to save his sacred life and then cleanse himself, and asks which is better: death without food, or the unclean meal.
shots.B12C140S05H02: The Chandala says each person must judge his own duty, and that anyone who calls dog meat clean would abstain from nothing.
shots.B12C140S05H03: Viswamitra says eating unclean food is sinful in general, but in mortal danger, without killing or deceit, it matters little.
shots.B12C140S05H04: The Chandala says the sage's reasoning disregards the Veda and Arya morality and dissolves the difference between clean and unclean food.
shots.B12C140S05H05: Viswamitra argues that forbidden food does not cause a grave fall, that the warnings against drink are only words, and that no sin destroys one's merit.
shots.B12C140S06H01: The Chandala says that a learned man who takes meat from such a wretch as himself acts against the good and will feel remorse.
shots.B12C140S06H02: Viswamitra takes the haunch, offers it to the gods and ancestors, eats it, and later wins great ascetic success; Bhishma concludes that a wise person may save his life in distress and then regain his merit.

B12C141.summary: Yudhishthira is appalled that Bhishma's teaching seems to excuse cruelty and to make robbers respectable, and asks whether any kingly rule may never be broken. Bhishma replies that duty must come from wisdom gathered from many sources rather than a one-sided reading of scripture, and that a king must be severe when the occasion demands and mild otherwise. He closes by saying that Brahmanas must always be honoured, since they can bring either great blessing or great harm.

scenes.B12C141S01: Yudhishthira's dismay at Bhishma's teaching on severity, Bhishma's answer on how duty is found, and his final advice to honour Brahmanas.

shots.B12C141S01H01: Yudhishthira says that if such cruelty can count as duty, nothing is forbidden and robbers would deserve respect, so he is bewildered and cannot follow the advice.
shots.B12C141S01H02: Bhishma replies that true duty comes from wisdom drawn from many sources, not from one-sided scripture, and that a king must be severe when needed and mild otherwise.
shots.B12C141S01H03: Yudhishthira asks whether any rule of kingship must never be broken.
shots.B12C141S01H04: Bhishma says Brahmanas must always be honoured, since they bring blessing when pleased and harm when angered.

B12C142.summary: Yudhishthira asks what merit comes from protecting a suppliant, and Bhishma says it is great, citing King Sivi and a pigeon that fed a foe who sought refuge with its own flesh. He then tells the story as Rama, son of Bhrigu, told it to King Muchukunda. A cruel fowler who lives by killing birds is caught in a storm and sets out to find shelter for the night beneath a great tree.

scenes.B12C142S01: The question about protecting suppliants, and the story of the cruel fowler, caught in a storm, who comes to the tree at night.

shots.B12C142S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what merit comes from sheltering a suppliant who seeks protection.
shots.B12C142S01H02: Bhishma says the merit is great, and cites King Sivi and a pigeon who fed a foe seeking refuge with its own flesh.
shots.B12C142S01H03: Yudhishthira asks how the pigeon did this and what it gained.
shots.B12C142S01H04: Bhishma says he will tell the story that Rama, son of Bhrigu, once told King Muchukunda, which cleanses the hearer of sin.
shots.B12C142S01H05: Rama describes a cruel fowler who kills birds for their meat and has been cast off by everyone, and who is caught in a violent storm while hunting in the forest; at night he rests under a great tree.

B12C143.summary: A pigeon lives with his family in a tree, and when his wife does not return on the stormy night he laments her absence. He praises the faithful wife as a man's true home, companion and support, and says a man without one should go to the forest.

scenes.B12C143S01: The pigeon's lament for his missing wife and his praise of a wife's value.

shots.B12C143S01H01: The pigeon waits in the tree for his wife, grieves that she has not returned, and praises a faithful wife as the true center of a home.

B12C144.summary: The she-pigeon, already caught in the fowler's cage, hears her husband's grief and urges him to welcome the fowler as a guest. She argues that refusing a suppliant is as sinful as killing a Brahmana or a cow, and tells him to take other wives if she dies.

scenes.B12C144S01: The captured she-pigeon hears her husband's words and advises him to show hospitality to the fowler.

shots.B12C144S01H01: Bhishma says the she-pigeon, captured by the fowler, hears her husband's lament and begins to reflect.
shots.B12C144S01H02: She reflects that a husband is a wife's highest deity, and urges her husband to rescue the suffering fowler by offering him hospitality, even telling him to remarry if she dies.

B12C145.summary: The pigeon welcomes the fowler and gives him warmth, but when the hungry fowler asks for food he has none. Bound by his duty to a guest, he throws himself into a fire he has lit so that he may be offered as food, and the fowler is overcome with grief.

scenes.B12C145S01: The pigeon's hospitality, his sacrifice of himself in the fire, and the fowler's grief.

shots.B12C145S01H01: The pigeon welcomes the fowler, lights a fire to warm him, has no food to offer, and throws himself into the flames as a meal for his guest, while the fowler is overcome with remorse.

B12C146.summary: Moved by the pigeon's death, the fowler blames himself and vows to give up his cruel trade for a life of strict penance. He throws away his weapons and cages and frees the captive she-pigeon.

scenes.B12C146S01: The fowler's remorse, his vow to live by righteousness, and his release of the she-pigeon.

shots.B12C146S01H01: The fowler reproaches himself, vows to abandon hunting and live by severe penance, throws away his weapons and cages, and frees the captive she-pigeon.

B12C147.summary: The she-pigeon mourns her husband and says life means nothing without him, then throws herself into the fire. She sees her husband in heaven on a celestial car, and the two ascend together as a reward for their merit.

scenes.B12C147S01: The she-pigeon's lament, her death in the fire, and the reunion of the pigeon couple in heaven.

shots.B12C147S01H01: The she-pigeon laments her husband, throws herself into the fire, finds him in heaven on a celestial car, and ascends with him.

B12C148.summary: Seeing the pigeon couple in heaven, the fowler resolves to win the same reward through austerity. He gives up food and deliberately runs into a forest fire, and is taken up to heaven for it. Bhishma ends by praising the protection of suppliants as a high merit and saying that hearing this tale cleanses sin.

scenes.B12C148S01: The fowler's resolve to imitate the pigeon, his death in a forest fire, his ascent to heaven, and Bhishma's closing praise of protecting suppliants.

shots.B12C148S01H01: The fowler, inspired by the pigeon couple, gives up food and runs into a forest fire, is cleansed by it and ascends to heaven, and Bhishma closes by praising the protection of suppliants and the cleansing power of the tale.

B12C149.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a person who sins through ignorance can be cleansed. Bhishma tells how King Janamejaya, son of Parikshit, killed a Brahmana, was abandoned by his priests and subjects, and wandered in penance. The sage Indrota, son of Sunaka, harshly rebukes the king when he comes to him for help.

scenes.B12C149S01: Yudhishthira's question about cleansing ignorant sin, and the story of Janamejaya's wanderings and the rebuke from Indrota.

shots.B12C149S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a person who sins out of ignorance can be cleansed.
shots.B12C149S01H02: Bhishma tells how Janamejaya, shunned by his priests and subjects after killing a Brahmana, wandered in penance until the sage Indrota, son of Sunaka, harshly rebuked him.

B12C150.summary: Janamejaya, tormented by remorse, begs the sage Saunaka for instruction and protection. Saunaka answers that folly is no cause for anger, but insists that the king repent, drop his pride, and honour Brahmanas, even if others mock him for it. The king swears never again to harm a Brahmana in thought, word or deed.

scenes.B12C150S01: Janamejaya's plea and repentance, and Saunaka's demand that the king honour Brahmanas, ending with the king's oath.

shots.B12C150S01H01: Janamejaya, burning with remorse, begs Saunaka to instruct and protect him and promises to honour Brahmanas again.
shots.B12C150S01H02: Saunaka says a fool's offences are no wonder, that a wise man pities rather than rages, and that the king should take refuge with Brahmanas.
shots.B12C150S01H03: Janamejaya says he repents his sins and will never again try to extinguish virtue.
shots.B12C150S01H04: Saunaka asks the king to lay down his pride, serve all creatures, and pledge not to injure Brahmanas, warning that his own kin and friends may mock him for speaking out.
shots.B12C150S01H05: Janamejaya swears, touching Saunaka's feet, that he will never again injure Brahmanas in thought, word or deed.

B12C151.summary: Saunaka tells the repentant king that a wise ruler must combine sternness with compassion, and recommends penance, gifts, sacred bathing places and graded remedies for each repeated sin. He cites the gods' question to Vrihaspati about how a righteous person cleanses sin, and Vrihaspati's answer that righteous acts done with understanding wash sin away. The sage then assists Janamejaya in the horse-sacrifice, and the purified king returns to his kingdom in splendour.

scenes.B12C151S01: Saunaka's long teaching on penance, sacred places and graded purification, with the gods' question to Vrihaspati and his answer, and the king's final purification.

shots.B12C151S01H01: Saunaka teaches that a wise king combines sternness with kindness, lists purifying acts and sacred bathing places, gives graded remedies for repeated sin, and recounts how the gods asked Vrihaspati how sin is cleansed.
shots.B12C151S01H02: Vrihaspati replies that righteous acts done with understanding wash away sin as a dirty cloth is cleaned, and that one should not boast of wrongdoing.
shots.B12C151S01H03: The sage helps Janamejaya perform the horse-sacrifice, and the cleansed king returns to his kingdom shining like fire.

B12C152.summary: Yudhishthira asks whether anyone has ever been restored to life after death. Bhishma tells how a Brahmana's only son dies, and how his kin at the cremation ground are argued back and forth between a vulture, who says the dead cannot return, and a jackal, who keeps them hoping. When the sun sets and the kin plead for help, Sankara appears and restores the child to life for a hundred years, showing that prayer and grace can overturn what seems final.

scenes.B12C152S01: A dead child is taken to the cremation ground, where a vulture tells the kin to leave and a jackal persuades them to turn back and reconsider.
scenes.B12C152S02: The kin return to the child, the vulture rejects any hope of revival and warns of night dangers, and the jackal keeps urging them to wait.
scenes.B12C152S03: The jackal insists the kin wait while the sun shines, and Sankara comes in answer to their prayer and restores the child.

shots.B12C152S01H01: Yudhishthira asks whether Bhishma has ever known anyone restored to life after death.
shots.B12C152S01H02: Bhishma tells how a Brahmana's only son dies, his kin carry the body to the cremation ground, a vulture urges them to go home, and a jackal then urges them to stay.
shots.B12C152S01H03: The vulture scolds the kin for listening to a jackal and urges them to leave the body and attend to their own conduct.
shots.B12C152S01H04: The jackal laments the kin's coldness, says they should show grief, and urges them to wait until the sun sets.
shots.B12C152S01H05: The vulture replies that no dead creature has ever come back to life, that every life span is fixed, and that grief grows at the sight of the body.
shots.B12C152S02H01: The jackal says they should not abandon the child, cites precedents of revival, and the kin return and weep over the body in their laps.
shots.B12C152S02H02: The vulture says the child cannot be revived except by a god's boon, and that all mortals travel the same road and should live righteously.
shots.B12C152S02H03: The jackal laments the miseries of the world and insists the child could still live, so the kin should not go away.
shots.B12C152S02H04: Bhishma explains that the jackal's soothing falsehoods kept the kin at the cremation ground.
shots.B12C152S02H05: The vulture warns that the place is dangerous at night and that the funeral rites must be finished before dark.
shots.B12C152S03H01: The jackal says the wilderness is safe while the sun still shines, and that the kin should wait in hope.
shots.B12C152S03H02: Bhishma tells how the vulture and jackal keep arguing until Sankara, moved by the kin's prayer, restores the child to life for a hundred years and satisfies both animals' hunger, and the family returns home in joy.

B12C153.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a weak man who has foolishly provoked a powerful enemy should act when that enemy comes to destroy him. Bhishma introduces the story of the Salmali tree, a great tree on the Himalaya that shelters elephants, birds and travellers. The sage Narada praises it and asks whether the wind god Pavana is its friend, since its branches are never broken by storms.

scenes.B12C153S01: Yudhishthira's question about a weak man who has provoked a powerful foe, and the opening of the tale of the Salmali tree and the wind god.

shots.B12C153S01H01: Yudhishthira asks how a weak, boastful man who has provoked a powerful foe should act when that foe attacks him in anger.
shots.B12C153S01H02: Bhishma introduces the tale of the Salmali tree on the Himalaya, which shelters many creatures, and tells how Narada praises it and asks whether the wind god Pavana is its friend.

B12C154.summary: The sage Narada tells the Salmali tree that the wind must protect it through some special friendship, since no other tree or mountain stands against the wind. The tree boasts that it is stronger than the wind and has defeated him before. Narada rebukes this arrogance and says he will report it to the wind-god.

scenes.B12C154S01: Narada's remark to the Salmali tree about the wind's protection, the tree's boast of strength, and Narada's rebuke.

shots.B12C154S01H01: Narada remarks that the wind must be a friend of the Salmali tree, since no tree or mountain can resist the wind.
shots.B12C154S01H02: The Salmali boasts that the wind is neither its friend nor its master, that its own might far exceeds the wind's, and that it has repeatedly beaten him.
shots.B12C154S01H03: Narada rebukes the tree for arrogance and folly, says the wind is the mightiest of beings, and promises to report the insults to the wind-god.

B12C155.summary: Narada reports the tree's insults to the wind-god, who comes to the Salmali in anger and threatens to show his power. The tree laughs at the threat and says that true strength lies in wisdom, so the wind promises a test the next day. Seeing that it is weaker, the tree decides to rely on its intelligence and resolves to protect itself from the wind's attack.

scenes.B12C155S01: Narada reports the tree to the wind-god, the wind's threat, and the tree's private reckoning that leads it to protect itself.

shots.B12C155S01H01: Bhishma says Narada reported the Salmali's words to the wind-god.
shots.B12C155S01H02: Narada tells the wind that the tree scorned him with many abusive words, and praises the wind as the mightiest of beings.
shots.B12C155S01H03: Bhishma says the wind-god, enraged, goes to the Salmali.
shots.B12C155S01H04: The wind-god warns the Salmali that he will show his power, and says the tree stands only because the Grandsire once rested beneath it.
shots.B12C155S01H05: The Salmali laughs, says that strength of understanding matters more than brute force, and the wind promises a test the next day; the tree then decides to rely on its wit and prepare against the wind.

B12C156.summary: The Salmali cuts off its own branches, leaving itself bare, and waits for the wind. The wind arrives, delighted to find the tree stripped, and says that the tree's own counsel has put it under his power. Ashamed and remorseful, the Salmali repents, and Bhishma concludes that a weak man should not provoke a powerful one and that the wise defeat the strong gradually, as the Pandava Arjuna defeated Duryodhana's army.

scenes.B12C156S01: The Salmali strips itself, the wind's mocking verdict, the tree's shame, and Bhishma's moral on provoking the powerful.

shots.B12C156S01H01: The Salmali cuts off its branches and leaves, and the wind comes towards it in rage, but is delighted to find the tree stripped bare.
shots.B12C156S01H02: The wind tells the tree that he would have done the same to it in anger, and that its own evil counsel has delivered it into his power.
shots.B12C156S01H03: Ashamed and remembering Narada's warning, the Salmali repents, and Bhishma draws the moral that a foolish person should not provoke the powerful, and that the wise overcome them by patience, citing Arjuna's victory over Duryodhana's armies.

B12C157.summary: Yudhishthira asks what is the source and foundation of sin. Bhishma replies that covetousness is the root of sin, giving rise to anger, lust, pride, deceit and countless other vices, and that it can never be satisfied. He then describes the good people who are free of covetousness, fearless, content and devoted to the good of all, and says they should be honoured and learned from.

scenes.B12C157S01: Yudhishthira's question about the source of sin, Bhishma's account of covetousness as its root, and his portrait of good people who are free of it.

shots.B12C157S01H01: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain the source and foundation of sin.
shots.B12C157S01H02: Bhishma says covetousness is the root of sin and of a long list of vices, can never be satisfied, and is overcome only by people who are free of greed, who are content, fearless and devoted to the good of others.

B12C158.summary: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain ignorance in detail. Bhishma says ignorance leads to sin, infamy and hell, and that attachment, hatred, vanity and many other faults are all called ignorance. He treats ignorance and covetousness as two sides of the same fault that grow and fade together, and says that kings such as Janaka gained heaven by restraining covetousness.

scenes.B12C158S01: Yudhishthira asks about ignorance, Bhishma defines it and links it to covetousness, and he urges the king to avoid greed.

shots.B12C158S01H01: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain covetousness and then ignorance in detail.
shots.B12C158S01H02: Bhishma says the ignorant man sins, earns infamy and sinks into hell, and that ignorance is the source of misery.
shots.B12C158S01H03: Yudhishthira asks for a full account of the origin, growth and effects of ignorance.
shots.B12C158S01H04: Bhishma says the faults he names are all ignorance, that ignorance and covetousness grow and fade together, and that kings such as Janaka gained heaven by restraining greed.

B12C159.summary: Yudhishthira asks which duties bring the highest merit. Bhishma answers that self-restraint is the highest duty, made up of forgiveness, patience, truthfulness, mildness, liberality and compassion, and leads the restrained person to freedom and the highest state. He admits one drawback, that others may think a self-restrained man weak, but says its merits far outweigh this. Yudhishthira, delighted, asks him to go on.

scenes.B12C159S01: Yudhishthira asks about the highest merit, Bhishma's praise of self-restraint and the path of the ascetic, and the king's renewed delight.

shots.B12C159S01H01: Yudhishthira asks which duties, among the many, bring the highest merit, both here and hereafter.
shots.B12C159S01H02: Bhishma says self-restraint is the highest duty, lists its marks such as forgiveness, truthfulness and mildness, describes the freedom and bliss of the restrained life, and notes that its only drawback is being mistaken for weakness.
shots.B12C159S01H03: Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira is delighted by the teaching and asks Bhishma to continue.

B12C160.summary: Bhishma teaches that penance is the root of all achievement, from the creation of the world and the Vedas to the status of the gods. He says that many kinds of wrongdoing can be cleansed by penance, and that abstaining from food is the highest form of it.

scenes.B12C160S01: Bhishma's teaching that penance is the root of all success and that abstaining from food is its highest form.

shots.B12C160S01H01: Bhishma teaches that penance underlies all creation, knowledge and success, that it cleanses even grave wrongs, and that abstaining from food is its highest form.

B12C161.summary: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain truth, its signs, how it is gained and what it brings. Bhishma calls truth the eternal duty and the foundation of all righteousness, and sets out its thirteen forms, such as impartiality, self-control and forgiveness. He ends by saying that truth outweighed a thousand horse-sacrifices when the two were weighed against each other.

scenes.B12C161S01: Yudhishthira's question about truth, and Bhishma's account of its thirteen forms and its supreme worth.

shots.B12C161S01H01: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain truth, its signs, how it is gained and what it brings.
shots.B12C161S01H02: Bhishma calls truth the eternal duty and foundation of righteousness, lists its thirteen forms with a short account of each, and says truth outweighed a thousand horse-sacrifices in the balance.

B12C162.summary: Yudhishthira asks about the origins of wrath, lust, envy, pride, malice and related vices. Bhishma calls these thirteen fierce foes that attack the heedless, and traces each to its source and cure, such as wrath springing from covetousness and dying away through forgiveness. He says tranquillity can subdue them all, and notes that Yudhishthira has already conquered them through respect for his elders.

scenes.B12C162S01: Yudhishthira's question about the vices, and Bhishma's account of their sources and the means of overcoming them.

shots.B12C162S01H01: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain the origin and cure of wrath, lust, envy, pride, malice and related vices.
shots.B12C162S01H02: Bhishma calls these thirteen vices fierce foes, traces each to its source and remedy, such as compassion, knowledge and tranquillity, and says Yudhishthira has already conquered them.

B12C163.summary: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to describe malevolent people, whom he says he has not known well. Bhishma portrays them as boastful, deceitful, covetous and quick to slander, who eat greedily alone and regret their gifts. He contrasts them with the generous man who first gives to Brahmanas and then shares with kin, and advises that the malevolent be avoided.

scenes.B12C163S01: Yudhishthira's question about malevolent people, and Bhishma's portrait of them set against the generous man.

shots.B12C163S01H01: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to describe the acts of malevolent people, whom he says he has not known well.
shots.B12C163S01H02: Bhishma describes the malevolent man as boastful, deceitful, covetous and slanderous, and says that the generous man who feeds Brahmanas and kin first is the opposite and should be sought out, while the malevolent should be avoided.

B12C164.summary: Bhishma sets rules for giving to Brahmanas: the learned and impoverished should be supported, the king may take wealth from those who refuse to fund sacrifices, and a hungry Brahmana may take a single meal in an emergency. He then lists the acts that make a Brahmana fallen and the expiation prescribed for each, from drinking liquor and killing a Brahmana to lesser faults, and says the gravest sins can be cleansed only by death. The chapter ends with a heading for the next section.

scenes.B12C164S01: Bhishma's long code on gifts, sacrifices and the king's duties to Brahmanas, with the penances for many kinds of wrongdoing.

shots.B12C164S01H01: Bhishma sets out rules for giving to Brahmanas, the king's duty to support them, and the expiations prescribed for each sin, from drinking liquor to killing a Brahmana.
shots.B12C164S01H02: A heading marks the start of Section CLXXIV.

B12C165.summary: Nakula asks Bhishma whether the bow or the sword is the foremost weapon, and who first made the sword. Bhishma recounts the creation of the world, the rise of the Danavas, and how Rudra, born from a sacrificial fire, slew them with the sword called Asi, which was then handed down through a line of kings to the Pandavas. He ranks the sword highest among weapons and says the bow was first made by Prithu.

scenes.B12C165S01: Nakula's question about weapons, and Bhishma's long account of the creation of the sword and its passage down the royal line.

shots.B12C165S01H01: Vaisampayana says Nakula, skilled with the sword, questions Bhishma as he lies on his bed of arrows.
shots.B12C165S01H02: Nakula asks whether the bow or the sword is the foremost weapon in battle, and who first created the sword and taught its use.
shots.B12C165S01H03: Vaisampayana says Bhishma, master of the bow, answers Nakula in fine words.
shots.B12C165S01H04: Bhishma recounts the creation of the world, the wicked Danavas, and how Rudra, using the sword Asi created by Brahman, destroyed them, before the sword passed through a line of kings down to Kripa and the Pandavas, while Prithu first made the bow.

B12C166.summary: After Bhishma falls silent, Yudhishthira asks his brothers and Vidura which of Virtue, Wealth and Desire is greatest and which the mind should serve. Vidura ranks Virtue highest, Wealth middling and Desire lowest, while Arjuna argues that Wealth is needed for the other two, the twins argue that Virtue and Wealth should be pursued in order, and Bhima argues that Desire is the foremost. Yudhishthira judges their arguments mistaken and concludes that liberation is the highest good, since all acts follow the will of the Ordainer.

scenes.B12C166S01: Yudhishthira's question about the three aims of life, and the views of Vidura and Arjuna.
scenes.B12C166S02: The views of Nakula, Sahadeva and Bhima, Yudhishthira's own conclusion on liberation, and the praise that follows.

shots.B12C166S01H01: After Bhishma falls silent, Yudhishthira asks his brothers and Vidura which of Virtue, Wealth and Desire is greatest and which the mind should serve.
shots.B12C166S01H02: Vidura says Virtue is supreme, Wealth middling and Desire lowest, and that one should live self-restrained and treat all creatures as oneself.
shots.B12C166S01H03: Vaisampayana says Arjuna speaks next, urged on by the drift of the king's question.
shots.B12C166S01H04: Arjuna argues that action brings Wealth, that Virtue and Desire cannot be won without it, and that even ascetics and believers seek it.
shots.B12C166S01H05: Vaisampayana says the twin sons of Madri, Nakula and Sahadeva, speak next.
shots.B12C166S02H01: Nakula and Sahadeva say that Wealth should be sought by vigorous means, that Virtue should come first, then Wealth, and then Desire.
shots.B12C166S02H02: Vaisampayana says the twins fall silent and Bhimasena begins to speak.
shots.B12C166S02H03: Bhima argues that Desire is the foremost of the three, since Virtue and Wealth both spring from it, and that the best man attends to all three.
shots.B12C166S02H04: Yudhishthira, after reflecting, judges their speeches mistaken, says that liberation is the highest good, and says that all things follow the Ordainer's will.
shots.B12C166S02H05: The brothers bow and praise Yudhishthira, who then turns again to the son of the foremost of rivers to ask about duties.

B12C167.summary: Yudhishthira asks what kinds of men make worthy friends, and Bhishma lists the men to avoid, such as the covetous, the cruel and the deceitful, and the men to befriend, such as the well-born, the grateful and the steady. Yudhishthira asks who the ungrateful injurers of friends are, and Bhishma begins a tale. It concerns a poor Brahmana named Gautama who, having taken up with a village of robbers and learned to kill cranes, is visited by an old friend who begs him to return to his proper duties.

scenes.B12C167S01: Yudhishthira's question about friendship, Bhishma's lists of those to avoid and those to befriend, and the opening of the tale of Gautama.

shots.B12C167S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what kinds of men make gentle and worthy friends, and who can help in good times and bad.
shots.B12C167S01H02: Bhishma lists the kinds of men to avoid as friends, including the covetous, the cruel and the deceitful, and then the kinds to befriend, such as the well-born, the grateful and the steady.
shots.B12C167S01H03: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to say who are the injurers of friends and the ungrateful.
shots.B12C167S01H04: Bhishma begins the tale of Gautama, a poor Brahmana without Vedic learning who settles in a robbers' village, learns to kill cranes, and is visited by an old friend who urges him to change his ways.

B12C168.summary: Gautama leaves the robbers' village for the sea, is separated from a merchant caravan when an elephant attacks it, and wanders into a beautiful forest. He rests beneath a great banyan tree, where the crane prince Rajadharman, son of Kasyapa, arrives at evening. Gautama, hungry, first eyes the crane as prey, but the crane greets him warmly as a guest.

scenes.B12C168S01: Gautama's journey after the elephant attack, his rest beneath the banyan, and his meeting with the crane who welcomes him.

shots.B12C168S01H01: Gautama sets out for the sea, is separated from a merchant caravan by an elephant attack, and comes to a beautiful forest and a great banyan, where he rests and then sees the crane Rajadharman arrive, eyeing him first as prey.
shots.B12C168S01H02: Rajadharman welcomes Gautama as a dear guest and offers him worship according to the rites.

B12C169.summary: Rajadharman hosts Gautama with food, flowers and a soft bed, and reveals that he is a son of Kasyapa. Learning that Gautama is poor and seeks wealth at sea, the crane promises to help, citing four ways of gaining wealth. He sends Gautama to his friend, the Rakshasa king Virupaksha, who he says will give him wealth.

scenes.B12C169S01: Rajadharman's hospitality, his promise to help the poor Brahmana, and his message sending Gautama to the Rakshasa king.

shots.B12C169S01H01: Gautama is amazed at the crane's sweet welcome and cannot stop staring at him.
shots.B12C169S01H02: Rajadharman introduces himself as a son of Kasyapa and welcomes his guest.
shots.B12C169S01H03: Rajadharman feeds Gautama, gives him a bed, learns he is poor, promises help, and sends him to his friend Virupaksha, a Rakshasa king who will give him wealth.

B12C170.summary: Virupaksha questions Gautama about his birth and practices, and Gautama gives only his name and race, adding that he lives among hunters with a Sudra widow as his wife. Out of loyalty to his friend the crane, the king honours Gautama at a great feast for a thousand Brahmanas and sends him away with gold. Gautama, laden with the gold, returns to the banyan, where the crane welcomes him, and he plots to kill the crane for its flesh.

scenes.B12C170S01: Virupaksha's questions and Gautama's answers, the king's feast and gifts of gold, and Gautama's ungrateful plot against the crane.

shots.B12C170S01H01: Virupaksha receives Gautama with honours and asks about his birth, practices and Vedic study, but Gautama gives only his name and race.
shots.B12C170S01H02: The king asks where Gautama lives and about his wife.
shots.B12C170S01H03: Gautama says he is a Middle-country Brahmana who lives among hunters and has married a Sudra widow.
shots.B12C170S01H04: The king, bound by his friend's request, holds a great feast for a thousand Brahmanas and gives Gautama gold; Gautama returns to the banyan, where the crane welcomes him, and Gautama, ungrateful, plots to kill the crane for food.

B12C171.summary: Gautama kills his sleeping crane host, roasts its flesh and flees with the gold. When the Rakshasa king Virupaksha finds that his friend has not returned, he sends his son, who finds the mutilated body and captures Gautama. The Rakshasas refuse to eat such an ungrateful man, since ingratitude, unlike other sins, has no expiation.

scenes.B12C171S01: Gautama's murder of the crane, the king's search and his order to kill the traitor, and the refusal of the Rakshasas and robbers to eat him.

shots.B12C171S01H01: Gautama kills the crane while it sleeps, flees with the gold, is found out by the Rakshasa king's son, and is cast aside by the Rakshasas and robbers, who will not eat an ungrateful man because ingratitude has no expiation.

B12C172.summary: Virupaksha has the crane burned on a pyre, and the goddess Surabhi's milk revives him. Indra explains that the crane was cursed for missing the Grandsire's assembly, and at the crane's plea Indra restores Gautama to life too, though Gautama is cursed to sink into hell for his ingratitude. Bhishma concludes that ingratitude is shameful and that friends should always be honoured.

scenes.B12C172S01: The crane's revival, Indra's explanation, Gautama's restoration and curse, and Bhishma's moral on gratitude to friends.

shots.B12C172S01H01: Virupaksha cremates the crane, Surabhi's milk revives him, Indra restores Gautama at the crane's request, and Bhishma closes with a long moral on gratitude to friends, ending with a question to Yudhishthira about what else he wishes to hear.
shots.B12C172S01H02: Vaisampayana begins to report Yudhishthira's reaction to Bhishma's words.
shots.B12C172S01H03: The sentence ends with Yudhishthira highly gratified by the teaching.

B12C173.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a person should set aside grief after losing wealth or a loved one, and Bhishma says that reflection can dissolve sorrow. He tells how a Brahmana consoled King Senajit, who was mourning his dead son, by reminding him that all must pass away and that grief is folly. The rest of the teaching continues in the next scene.

scenes.B12C173S01: The heading of the Mokshadharma Parva, Yudhishthira's questions on duty and grief, and the Brahmana's first words to King Senajit.
scenes.B12C173S02: Senajit asks what wisdom ends grief; the Brahmana answers with a long teaching on impermanence and detachment, and tells the story of Pingala.

shots.B12C173S01H02: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to set out the duties of those in each of the four modes of life.
shots.B12C173S01H03: Bhishma says religion has many paths, and that the inner penance which frees the soul brings its fruit in this world, so every wise person should seek liberation.
shots.B12C173S01H04: Yudhishthira asks how a person can kill grief at the loss of wealth, a wife, a son or a father.
shots.B12C173S01H05: Bhishma tells how a Brahmana, seeing King Senajit grieve for his dead son, reminds him that everyone will one day leave this world and that grief is folly.
shots.B12C173S02H01: Senajit asks what wisdom and penance could keep a man from grief.
shots.B12C173S02H02: The Brahmana argues that all creatures are bound by sorrow, that nothing is truly one's own, that joy and sorrow follow each other, and that destiny and freedom from desire bring peace.
shots.B12C173S02H03: The Brahmana tells how the courtesan Pingala, whose lover failed to come, found peace by casting off hope and desire.
shots.B12C173S02H04: Bhishma says that Senajit is persuaded by these words, sets aside his grief and grows happy.

B12C174.summary: Yudhishthira asks what good thing one should seek while time carries life away. Bhishma tells of a learned Brahmana's son, Medhavin, who asks his father how to act when death is always near. The father gives the usual stages of life, but the son warns that death and decay surround every creature, and urges pursuit of truth and renunciation over ritual.

scenes.B12C174S01: Yudhishthira's question, and the son's first question to his father about how to live when life is short, with the father's reply on the four stages of life.
scenes.B12C174S02: The son's warning that death is near and his call to truth and renunciation, with Bhishma's closing advice to Yudhishthira.

shots.B12C174S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what good thing should be sought while time carries every creature toward death.
shots.B12C174S01H02: Bhishma introduces the story of Medhavin, a clever son of a Vedic Brahmana, who asks his father how to live when life is so brief.
shots.B12C174S01H03: The son asks his father to set out the duties and their rewards so that he can follow them.
shots.B12C174S01H04: The father lays out the stages of life: study the Vedas, have sons to honour the ancestors, perform the sacrifices, and then retire to the forest to meditate.
shots.B12C174S01H05: The son asks how his father can speak so calmly while the world is under attack from death and decay.
shots.B12C174S02H01: The father asks what he means by the world being assailed and what the irresistible dangers are.
shots.B12C174S02H02: The son replies that death and decay surround every creature, that each night shortens life, and that the wise should pursue truth and renounce ties to village life rather than perform elaborate animal sacrifices.
shots.B12C174S02H03: Bhishma urges Yudhishthira to act as the father did after hearing the son's words, devoted to truth.

B12C175.summary: Yudhishthira asks whence happiness and misery come to rich and poor who follow different practices. Bhishma gives verses sung by a Brahmana, miserable with a bad wife and hunger, who says that happiness and sorrow come from destiny and that poverty freed from desire brings true ease, while the wealthy grow anxious and proud. Bhishma concludes that renunciation is the highest good, as he heard from a Brahmana at Hastinapur.

scenes.B12C175S01: Yudhishthira's question, and the verses of Sampaka praising poverty and renunciation over wealth.

shots.B12C175S01H01: Yudhishthira asks whence happiness and misery come to rich and poor alike, when they follow different practices.
shots.B12C175S01H02: Bhishma gives verses of Sampaka, sung by a miserable Brahmana, saying that happiness and sorrow come from destiny, that poverty freed from desire is peaceful, that wealth brings anxiety and pride, and that renunciation is the highest good.

B12C176.summary: Yudhishthira asks what a man who craves wealth and cannot find it should do to be happy. Bhishma says the happy man is even-minded toward joy and sorrow, honour and insult, speaks truth, and seeks no worldly gain. He tells the story of Manki, whose two new bulls are carried off by a camel, and who concludes that destiny rules wealth and that desire is the real enemy. Manki then renounces his desire and attains a state of immortal peace.

scenes.B12C176S01: Yudhishthira's question about desire for wealth, and the story of Manki, who renounces desire after losing his bulls to a camel.

shots.B12C176S01H01: Yudhishthira asks what a man should do for happiness when he craves wealth and cannot find it.
shots.B12C176S01H02: Bhishma says the happy man is even-minded and truthful and free from attachment, and tells how Manki, after a camel drags off his two bulls, reasons that destiny governs wealth and then renounces desire for good.

B12C177.summary: Bhishma cites King Janaka, who says he owns nothing even if his kingdom burns, and the sage Vodhya, who names six teachers of tranquillity. Vodhya's teachers are the courtesan Pingala, an osprey, a snake, the bee, a shaft-maker and a maiden with an anklet. Each one shows that hope agitates the heart and that living free of hope, possessions and strife brings peace.

scenes.B12C177S01: Janaka's saying, Yayati's son's question to the sage Vodhya, and Vodhya's six teachers of tranquillity.

shots.B12C177S01H01: Bhishma cites King Janaka, who says his wealth is unlimited yet he owns nothing that a fire could take from him, and tells how the royal son of Nahusha, Yayati, asks the sage Vodhya for the secret of tranquillity.
shots.B12C177S01H02: Vodhya replies that he follows others' teaching without instructing, and names six teachers: Pingala, the osprey, the snake, the bee, the shaft-maker and the maiden.
shots.B12C177S01H03: Bhishma explains that hope is the great agitator, and that each teacher shows a lesson, such as the osprey finding peace when it gives up its meat, the snake living in another's home, and the maiden wandering alone like a lone anklet.

B12C178.summary: Yudhishthira asks how a person can live free of grief and reach a good end. Bhishma tells how King Prahlada questions a serene wandering Brahmana, who lives by the Ajagara vow, taking whatever food and rest come to him without desire or grief. The sage explains that all creatures are subject to death and change, so one should accept what comes, and Bhishma concludes that such a man passes his days in great delight.

scenes.B12C178S01: Yudhishthira's question, and Prahlada's conversation with the wandering sage who lives by the Ajagara vow of contentment.

shots.B12C178S01H01: Yudhishthira asks by what conduct a person can live free of grief and reach an excellent end.
shots.B12C178S01H02: Bhishma tells how King Prahlada questions a wise and serene wandering Brahmana.
shots.B12C178S01H03: Prahlada praises the Brahmana's freedom from desire and calm, and asks what learning and conduct have brought it about.
shots.B12C178S01H04: The Brahmana replies that all creatures meet death and change without a clear cause, so he takes whatever food and rest come, and keeps the Ajagara vow, which is free of fear and desire.
shots.B12C178S01H05: Bhishma says that one who casts off attachment, fear and desire and follows this vow passes his days in great delight.

B12C179.summary: Yudhishthira asks whether kinsmen, action, wealth or wisdom should be a person's refuge, and Bhishma says wisdom is the highest refuge. He tells how Indra, disguised as a jackal, speaks to the despairing Brahmana Kasyapa, who has been knocked down by a careless Vaisya and wants to end his life. Indra persuades him that a human birth and a Brahmana's status are precious, and that his pride in argument had caused his fall, and Kasyapa worships Indra and goes home.

scenes.B12C179S01: Yudhishthira's question on refuge, Bhishma's praise of wisdom, and the story of Indra's disguised rebuke to Kasyapa.

shots.B12C179S01H01: Yudhishthira asks whether kinsmen, action, wealth or wisdom should be a person's refuge.
shots.B12C179S01H02: Bhishma says wisdom is the highest refuge and recounts how Indra, disguised as a jackal, talks the despairing Brahmana Kasyapa out of suicide, reminds him of the value of his human birth, and names his past pride as the cause of his fall.

B12C180.summary: Yudhishthira asks whether gifts, sacrifices, penances and service to teachers bring wisdom and happiness. Bhishma answers that a mind swayed by desire and anger runs toward sin, and that deeds bear their fruit in later lives, following a person as his shadow does. Charity and faith bring prosperity and unbelief brings suffering, but a penitent person can cleanse the past through penance and knowledge.

scenes.B12C180S01: Yudhishthira's question, and Bhishma's teaching on the fruits of action and on the way to cleansing past sins.

shots.B12C180S01H01: Yudhishthira asks whether gifts, sacrifices, penances and service to teachers bring wisdom and high felicity.
shots.B12C180S01H02: Bhishma says that desire and anger lead to sin and suffering, that deeds bear fruit in later lives as a shadow follows its owner, and that repentance and penance can cleanse the past.

B12C181.summary: Yudhishthira asks who created the universe, what creatures are, and where the dead go. Bhishma passes on the teaching that the sage Bhrigu gave to Bharadwaja: a primeval being called Manasa creates the elements, a lotus, and Brahman, and the universe is his body. Bhrigu then describes the boundless sky and its layers of water and fire, and explains that the earth is the lotus whose centre is Mount Sumeru.

scenes.B12C181S01: Yudhishthira's questions on creation, and Bhrigu's account of the primeval being Manasa and the origin of the elements and Brahman.
scenes.B12C181S02: Bhrigu's account of the boundless sky and the layers of water and fire, and his explanation of the lotus that Brahman sprang from.

shots.B12C181S01H01: Yudhishthira asks who created the universe, how creatures and castes came about, and where the dead go.
shots.B12C181S01H02: Bhishma introduces the teaching that the sage Bhrigu gave to Bharadwaja, who found him seated on Mount Kailasa.
shots.B12C181S01H03: Bharadwaja asks Bhrigu who created the universe and its creatures, where castes and the moral order come from, and where the dead go.
shots.B12C181S01H04: Bhrigu describes a primeval being, Manasa, who creates the elements, a lotus and Brahman, and whose body is the universe itself.
shots.B12C181S01H05: Bharadwaja asks Bhrigu how far the sky, the horizons, the earth and the wind extend.
shots.B12C181S02H01: Bhrigu says the sky is infinite and has many regions, with layers of water and fire beyond the reach of the sun and moon, and that even the gods cannot measure it.
shots.B12C181S02H02: Bharadwaja asks why Brahman is called the first-born if he came from the lotus.
shots.B12C181S02H03: Bhrigu says the earth is the lotus, and that Mount Sumeru forms its centre, where Brahman created the worlds.

B12C182.summary: Bharadwaja asks how the creator, dwelling in Meru, made the diverse objects of the world. Bhrigu says the creator first made water, which sustains life, and that earth and mountains are solidified water. He then tells how seers who fasted for a thousand years heard a celestial voice describe the sequence: space, then water, then wind from water's pressure, then fire from friction, and finally earth from solidified fire.

scenes.B12C182S01: Bharadwaja's question about creation, Bhrigu's account of water as the first creation, and the celestial voice describing how the elements arose.

shots.B12C182S01H01: Bharadwaja asks how the creator, dwelling in Meru, made the diverse objects of the world.
shots.B12C182S01H02: Bhrigu says the creator first made water to sustain life, and that earth, mountains and clouds are all forms of solidified water.
shots.B12C182S01H03: Bharadwaja asks how water, fire, wind and earth first arose.
shots.B12C182S01H04: Bhrigu tells how seers who fasted for a thousand years heard a celestial voice describe how space, water, wind, fire and earth came into being in turn.

B12C183.summary: Bharadwaja asks why only the five primal elements are called creatures. Bhrigu answers that they are called great because they pervade all things, and that all bodies and senses are built from them. Bharadwaja objects that trees show none of the signs of the elements, but Bhrigu argues that trees feel, see, smell and taste, and so have life, and he then describes how the elements and their properties appear in living bodies.

scenes.B12C183S01: Bharadwaja's question about the five elements, Bhrigu's answer on how they make up all things, and the argument over whether trees contain them.

shots.B12C183S01H01: Bharadwaja asks why only the five primal elements are called creatures, when Brahman made thousands.
shots.B12C183S01H02: Bhrigu says the five elements are called great because they pervade all things, with wind as activity, space as sound, fire as heat, water as liquid and earth as solid matter, and the senses partake of them.
shots.B12C183S01H03: Bharadwaja objects that trees show none of the elements' signs of hearing, seeing, heat, motion or sense, so they cannot be made of the five elements.
shots.B12C183S01H04: Bhrigu answers that trees have space, heat, feeling, hearing, sight, scent and taste, so they live, and describes how the elements, the senses, the breaths and the properties of scent, taste, form, touch and sound appear in living bodies.

B12C184.summary: Bharadwaja asks how bodily heat dwells in the body and how wind moves it. Bhrigu explains that heat lies in the head and works with the breaths to drive life, the senses, excretion, digestion and bodily movement. He adds that yogins who hold the soul within the brain can reach Brahma through the main channel of the body.

scenes.B12C184S01: Bharadwaja's question on bodily heat and wind, and Bhrigu's account of the breaths and the path of the yogins.

shots.B12C184S01H01: Bharadwaja asks how bodily heat dwells in the body and how wind enables it to move and act.
shots.B12C184S01H02: Bhrigu explains that heat lies in the head, that the five breaths govern life, the senses, excretion, the joints and digestion, and that yogins reach Brahma by holding the soul in the brain.

B12C185.summary: Bharadwaja objects to the account: if life were only wind or inner heat, it would merge back into outer air or fire at death, and nothing would remain of the person once the elements separate. He asks what knows, hears or speaks after such a separation, doubts that a gift of a cow helps the dead, and concludes that everything arises from seeds and perishes at death.

scenes.B12C185S01: Bharadwaja's sceptical objections about life, death and the usefulness of gifts after death.

shots.B12C185S01H01: Bharadwaja objects that life, if it were only wind or inner heat, would merge back into outer air or fire at death, that gifts to Brahmanas could not help the dead, and that everything comes from seeds and perishes.

B12C186.summary: Bhrigu says the living creature is not destroyed with the body but passes into another form, as fire vanishes into space when its fuel is consumed. Bharadwaja objects that the analogy fails, and asks who feels pain, hears or sees once the body is only a union of the elements. Bhrigu replies that an inner Soul witnesses the senses, migrates from body to body, and survives the body's dissolution.

scenes.B12C186S01: The debate on whether the living creature survives death, with Bhrigu's fire analogy, Bharadwaja's objections and Bhrigu's teaching on the inner Soul.

shots.B12C186S01H01: Bhrigu says the living creature is not destroyed with the body, but passes into another form, as fire cannot be seen once its fuel is consumed.
shots.B12C186S01H02: Bharadwaja objects that fire is simply extinguished when its fuel runs out, so that what has no action or trace has truly perished.
shots.B12C186S01H03: Bhrigu replies that fire merges into space, that the vital heat sustaining the breaths leaves the body, and that the body falls back to earth while the elements take form only in living creatures.
shots.B12C186S01H04: Bharadwaja asks what the living agent is, if the body is only five elements, since the agent seems not to hear or see when the mind is elsewhere and feels nothing in sleep.
shots.B12C186S01H05: Bhrigu says the mind too is made of the elements, that an inner Soul witnesses the senses and migrates from body to body after death, and that the Supreme Soul creates the worlds.

B12C187.summary: Bhrigu describes creation: Brahman first made the Prajapatis, then Truth, Duty, Penance and the Vedas, and then all beings, including the four classes, each assigned a colour. Bharadwaja objects that all men share the same passions and bodily functions, so colour cannot separate them into classes. Bhrigu replies that all men were once Brahmanas and that conduct made some Kshatriyas, Vaisyas or Sudras, while those who fell from knowledge became Pisachas, Rakshasas and other beings.

scenes.B12C187S01: Bhrigu's account of Brahman's first creations and the colours of the four classes, Bharadwaja's objection, and Bhrigu's explanation of how the classes arose from conduct.

shots.B12C187S01H01: Bhrigu says Brahman first made the Prajapatis, then Truth, Duty, Penance and the Vedas, and then all beings, with white for Brahmanas, red for Kshatriyas, yellow for Vaisyas and black for Sudras.
shots.B12C187S01H02: Bharadwaja objects that colour cannot tell men apart, since all share the same passions and bodily functions, and that the creatures are too many to sort into classes.
shots.B12C187S01H03: Bhrigu says all men were once Brahmanas, that conduct turned some into Kshatriyas, Vaisyas or Sudras, that those who lost knowledge became Pisachas, Rakshasas and other beings, and that the Rishis made a lasting creation by their penance and yoga.

B12C188.summary: Bharadwaja asks by what acts one becomes a Brahmana, a Kshatriya, a Vaisya or a Sudra. Bhrigu describes the Brahmana by his purifying rites, Vedic study, daily duties, hospitality and truthfulness, the Kshatriya as a warrior who studies and gives gifts, the Vaisya as a cattle-keeper or farmer, and the Sudra as one unclean in conduct who ignores the Vedas. He ends by urging mastery over greed and anger, and renunciation of the self, as the path to Brahma.

scenes.B12C188S01: Bharadwaja's question on the marks of each class, and Bhrigu's description of the Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vaisya and Sudra and the path to Brahma.

shots.B12C188S01H01: Bharadwaja asks by what acts one becomes a Brahmana, a Kshatriya, a Vaisya or a Sudra.
shots.B12C188S01H02: Bhrigu describes each class by its conduct, from the Brahmana's rites, study and truthfulness to the Sudra's uncleanness, then urges control of greed and anger and renunciation as the way to Brahma.

B12C189.summary: Bhrigu teaches that truth is Brahma and the root of penance and creation, that untruth leads to darkness, and that happiness is the aim of all action. Bharadwaja doubts that happiness is the highest aim, since Brahma and Shiva, who conquered desire, do not seek it. Bhrigu replies that those ruled by anger and greed suffer disease, death and loss, while heaven knows no hunger, thirst or sin, so happiness is the highest goal.

scenes.B12C189S01: Bhrigu's teaching that truth leads to light and happiness, Bharadwaja's doubt, and Bhrigu's reply on the miseries of the untruthful.

shots.B12C189S01H01: Bhrigu says truth is Brahma and the root of penance and creation, that untruth leads to darkness, and that happiness is the aim toward which all action tends.
shots.B12C189S01H02: Bharadwaja doubts that happiness is the highest aim, since Brahma and Shiva, who conquered desire, do not pursue it.
shots.B12C189S01H03: Bhrigu replies that those ruled by anger and greed suffer disease, death and loss, while heaven has no hunger, thirst or sin, so happiness is the highest goal.

B12C190.summary: Bharadwaja asks what gifts, righteousness, conduct, penance, Vedic study and fire offerings bring. Bhrigu says offerings burn sin, study brings peace, gifts bring pleasure, and gifts to the good follow the giver after death. He then describes the stages of life set down by Brahman: the student under a teacher, the householder who supports the others and enjoys family, wealth and pleasure, and the forest dweller, each with its own duties.

scenes.B12C190S01: Bharadwaja's questions on the rewards of gift, conduct and penance, the duties of each person, and the four modes of life.
scenes.B12C190S02: Bhrigu describes the student's discipline, the householder's life and duties, and the forest life.

shots.B12C190S01H01: Bharadwaja asks what gifts, righteousness, conduct, penance, Vedic study and fire offerings each bring.
shots.B12C190S01H02: Bhrigu says offerings burn sin, study brings peace, gifts bring pleasure and penance heaven, and gifts to the good follow the giver after death.
shots.B12C190S01H03: Bharadwaja asks which duties belong to whom, what marks duty, and how many kinds there are.
shots.B12C190S01H04: Bhrigu says the wise who perform their duties win heaven, while those who neglect them are led into folly.
shots.B12C190S01H05: Bharadwaja asks Bhrigu to set out the four modes of life that Brahman laid down, with the practices for each.
shots.B12C190S02H01: Bhrigu describes the student's discipline under his teacher, the householder's family life and enjoyments, and the forest dweller's simple life, and praises the householder who lives modestly.

B12C191.summary: Bhrigu describes the austere life of forest hermits, who sleep on bare ground, live on roots and leaves, and endure heat and cold through penance. He then describes wandering renouncers who give up home, possessions and family and do no harm to any creature. Bharadwaja asks about the region beyond the known world, and Bhrigu describes a righteous northern land across the Himalaya, contrasting it with this world as the field where good and evil deeds bear fruit.

scenes.B12C191S01: Bhrigu's descriptions of forest hermits and wandering renouncers, Bharadwaja's question about the northern region, Bhrigu's account of it, and Bhishma's closing.

shots.B12C191S01H01: Bhrigu describes forest hermits who bathe, perform daily rites, live on wild roots and fruit, sleep on the bare ground and endure heat and cold until their bodies waste away.
shots.B12C191S01H02: Bhrigu describes wandering renouncers who give up fire, wealth, family and comforts, harm no creature, stay only briefly in any place, and take alms only in their bowls.
shots.B12C191S01H03: Bharadwaja asks Bhrigu to describe a region beyond this world that he has heard of but never seen.
shots.B12C191S01H04: Bhrigu describes a sacred northern land beyond the Himalaya where people are righteous, free from disease and sin, and where the fruits of deeds are visible, while this world is the field of action where good and evil are both found.
shots.B12C191S01H05: Bhishma says Bhrigu finished his teaching, Bharadwaja worshipped him, and Bhishma asks Yudhishthira what more he wishes to hear.
